results.summary: Chasey is a maze game where the player controls a character to escape a ghost, rendered over VGA at 640x480 resolution. It uses five active-high buttons for reset and directional movement, and outputs VGA color and sync signals through a Tiny VGA PMOD. The design is implemented in SystemVerilog and runs on a 25 MHz clock. Silicon test results are not provided, so correct operation on hardware is not confirmed.

This project implements a Direct Memory Access (DMA) controller that processes transfer descriptors from a ring buffer, configured over SPI. It includes an SPI register interface, a ring manager, a descriptor fetcher and data mover, and an interrupt output for ring-empty and error conditions. The design is tested by connecting an external SPI master and writing configuration and descriptor tail pointer registers; internal activity is monitored via probe outputs. For this tapeout, an internal memory stub replaces an AXI4 master, and no external hardware beyond an SPI master is required. The design is notable for its autonomous descriptor processing and consolidated interrupt scheme.

This design displays a bouncing logo on a VGA monitor, using the standard Tiny VGA pinout for color and sync signals. It is a beginner project with minimal documentation, described only as 'v1 logo bouncing' with a test note of 'Test 123'. The implementation is in Verilog and requires a VGA monitor and a Tiny VGA PMOD for external connection. No silicon test results or detailed functionality are provided.

This is an 8-bit RISC CPU with an ALU, registers, and data memory, designed to execute 16-bit instructions provided externally. The instruction bits are mapped to the input pins, and the CPU's 8-bit output is presented on the output pins. The design is implemented in Verilog and runs on a 5 MHz clock. No documentation on testing or external hardware is provided, and silicon results are not mentioned.

The SAP 8 Bit Computer is a processor implementing a 16-instruction, 8-bit ISA inspired by SAP architectures, with support for memory access, immediate operations, arithmetic/logic, control flow, and basic I/O. It operates at a very low clock of 10 Hz, making its state visible on LEDs. Testing requires DIP switches or buttons for program entry, LEDs for output observation, and optionally a logic analyzer or 7-segment display. No external hardware is strictly required, but these aids are recommended for easier testing. The design is notable for its simplicity and educational value, emulating early computer architectures.

This project is a 16-bit one-hot ring counter that sequentially activates its outputs at the clock rate, with a single high bit shifting through 16 outputs. The first 8 outputs are on dedicated output pins, and the next 8 are on bidirectional pins configured as outputs. It requires only a clock source and reset button, with LEDs for visual feedback; the Tiny Tapeout demo board provides these. The design is simple and useful for educational demonstrations of shift registers and one-hot encoding. No silicon test results are provided.

DOTTEE is a demoscene demo that generates VGA graphics and audio, racing the beam to produce a 640x480 60fps output with music synthesized via a 1-bit sigma-delta DAC. It renders an array of colored circles using distance calculations and constructs a 'DOTTEE' logo with a Tiny Tapeout-inspired 'TT'. The demo loops after 4096 frames and includes a noise generator for percussive sounds. It requires a Tiny VGA PMOD and a TT Audio PMOD for output, and is notable for its efficient 1-tile implementation and participation in the Tiny Tapeout Demoscene Competition.

This mixed-signal project features a voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) implemented as a current-starved ring oscillator, with its control voltage set by a 9-bit DAC. The VCO output drives a 5-bit counter and clock divider stages, providing divided outputs. It operates without an external clock and is tested by applying power and varying the 9-bit DAC input to observe frequency changes on the outputs, with an oscilloscope recommended for monitoring. The design demonstrates analog-digital integration using standard cells and is notable for its wide frequency range and digital controllability. Limitations include potential instability at extreme control voltages.

This design is a quantized INT8 multiply-accumulate (MAC) engine with bias, activation, and quantizer post-processing, intended as a co-processor for neural-network inference on a microcontroller. It is controlled via a 4-wire SPI slave interface and provides status outputs including idle, busy, result-valid, and accumulator overflow. Testing requires an SPI master host, and optional logic analyzer; no other external hardware is needed. The chip is self-contained and notable for its integrated post-processing pipeline, but it has no silicon test results reported.

The Tiny TPU Systolic Array is a small matrix multiplication accelerator based on a systolic array of processing elements, each performing multiply-accumulate operations. It is controlled via SPI, with results sent back over MISO. The design can be tested using a cocotb testbench that drives SPI commands and observes serial output, and no external hardware is required beyond the standard Tiny Tapeout pins. Notable for its systolic architecture and potential for neural network acceleration, but no silicon test results are provided.
